title: The first two sentences on Study 2 contradict the third and Figure 1(b)
location: published p. 2, Figure 1(b); p. 3, the paragraph on Study 2
published: When their party controls 60 percent of seats (compared with 40 percent), Republicans prefer a candidate who is more conservative. When their party controls 60 percent of seats (compared with 40 percent), Democrats prefer a candidate who is less liberal. Surprisingly (to me at least), subjects of both parties want more moderate candidates when the Republicans are in the majority and more extreme candidates when the Democrats are in the majority.
note: Figure 1(b) comes from the book's 2014 survey, in which the seat shares were randomized (question 58), and reproduces within rounding from the review's own script, which is in the project's files and was not deposited. Its scale runs from 1 = Extreme Republican to 5 = Extreme Democrat. Moving from a Democratic to a Republican majority changes Republicans' preference by 0.212 (95% interval -0.005 to 0.429) and Democrats' by -0.121 (95% interval -0.319 to 0.076). So under their own party's majority Republicans lean toward the moderate end and Democrats toward the liberal end, as the third sentence and the figure say. The first two sentences state the reverse. They would agree with the figure if they read 'less conservative' and 'more liberal', and this item corrects nothing until the author confirms that wording. Both intervals cover zero. The same design in the 2018 survey (question 401), which the review does not plot, gives the signs of the first two sentences, Republicans -0.049 (95% interval -0.248 to 0.151) and Democrats 0.212 (95% interval -0.006 to 0.429), and those intervals cover zero too.
